messages.content: What's the total number of possible arrangements in a chess game?

function.name: boardgame_calculate_score

message.content:
The number of distinct positions that can arise in a legal game of chess is astronomically large.  In 1950 Claude Shannon famously estimated that the “Shannon number” – a lower bound on the size of the game tree – is on the order of

\[
10^{43}\text{–}10^{50}
\]

legal positions.  More recent computational studies have refined this estimate to roughly

\[
\boxed{10^{43}\text{ to }10^{44}\text{ distinct positions}}
\]

(about 10 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000 000).  

If you’re asking about the total number of possible games (i.e., sequences of moves), that number is even larger—roughly \(10^{120}\) different games.  But for the sheer count of unique board arrangements, the figure above is the accepted estimate.
